lede: Every bottle of solution in a laboratory carries a label such as 0.2 mol/dm³: how much substance is dissolved in each cubic decimetre. The second half asks a different question. When you make a chemical, how much of what you start with ends up in the product you actually want?
can: Calculate a concentration in mol/dm³ from a mass of solute and a volume of solution.
Work out the moles or the mass of solute in a volume of known concentration.
Calculate an atom economy from a balanced equation and explain why a high one matters.

md: Make squash twice: one spoonful of powder in a small glass, then one spoonful in a full jug. Same powder, very different drinks, because the same amount is shared through more water. Chemists need to say exactly how strong a solution is, so they count the dissolved substance in moles and share it out per cubic decimetre.

prompt: Two solutions each contain 0.1 mol of salt. One has a volume of 250 cm³ and the other 1000 cm³. Which is more concentrated?
explain: The same 0.1 mol is packed into a quarter of the volume, so every dm³ of it holds four times as much. That is exactly what concentration measures.

md:
**Concentration** is the number of moles of the dissolved substance, the **solute**, in each cubic decimetre of solution:
**concentration (mol/dm³) = moles ÷ volume (dm³)**
A cubic decimetre is a cube 10 cm along each edge, so 1 dm³ = 1000 cm³, which is one litre. Read mol/dm³ as *moles per cubic decimetre*.

title: Why moles, not grams
md: Reactions happen particle by particle, and a mole of any substance is the same number of particles. So two solutions with the same concentration in mol/dm³ carry the same number of reacting particles in every dm³, whatever is dissolved. That is why CCEA asks for mol/dm³.

explain: 1000, because the cube is 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm. Every conversion in this lesson uses that one number.

md:
Laboratory volumes are measured in cm³, but the formula needs dm³. So the first line of every concentration calculation is the conversion, written on its own: **divide cm³ by 1000**.
Leave the volume in cm³ and a concentration comes out a thousand times too small, while a number of moles comes out a thousand times too big. Either answer should look odd to you straight away.

explain: 75 ÷ 1000 = 0.075 dm³. A dm³ is the bigger unit, so the number must get smaller; if you reached 75 000, you multiplied instead of dividing.

md:
**The question.** 5.85 g of sodium chloride, NaCl, is dissolved in water and made up to 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration in mol/dm³.
**Line 1, the volume.** 250 ÷ 1000 = 0.250 dm³.
**Line 2, the moles.** The Mr of NaCl is 23 + 35.5 = 58.5, so moles = mass ÷ Mr = 5.85 ÷ 58.5.

prompt: Sodium chloride has Mr 58.5. How many moles are there in 5.85 g of it?
explain: 5.85 ÷ 58.5 = 0.100 mol. Keep it on its own line: in the exam it is a mark of its own even if the next line slips.

md:
**Line 3, the concentration.** moles ÷ volume = 0.100 ÷ 0.250 = **0.400 mol/dm³**.
Write all three lines even when the arithmetic feels easy. A slip in line 2 then costs one mark, not three, because the examiner follows your working forward.

prompt: 0.0400 mol of copper(II) sulfate is dissolved to make 0.200 dm³ of solution. What is its concentration in mol/dm³?
explain: 0.0400 ÷ 0.200 = 0.200 mol/dm³. The volume was already in dm³, so there was nothing to convert: check the unit before you divide.

md:
When the concentration is known, rearrange: **moles = concentration × volume (dm³)**. If the question wants grams, finish with **mass = moles × Mr**.
For example, the mass of potassium nitrate, $\ce{KNO3}$, in 250 cm³ of a 0.400 mol/dm³ solution. Volume: 0.250 dm³. Moles: 0.400 × 0.250 = 0.100 mol. Mr = 39 + 14 + 48 = 101. Mass = 0.100 × 101 = **10.1 g**.

prompt: How many moles of solute are there in 50.0 cm³ of a 2.00 mol/dm³ solution?
explain: Convert first: 50.0 cm³ = 0.0500 dm³. Then 2.00 × 0.0500 = 0.100 mol. Multiplying by 50.0 instead gives 100 mol, far more than a small beaker could ever hold.

explain: The moles of solute stay the same but they are shared through a bigger volume, so each dm³ holds fewer moles.

md:
Making a chemical usually makes something else too. **Atom economy** measures how much of the products' mass is the product you want:
**atom economy = (mass of desired product ÷ total mass of products) × 100**
Heating limestone to make lime: $\ce{CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2}$. Of every 100 mass units, 56 become calcium oxide and 44 leave as carbon dioxide, so the atom economy is 56%.

title: Why the equation settles it
md: Mass is conserved, so the products weigh as much as the reactants. The balanced equation therefore fixes the atom economy before anyone lights a burner: a reaction that makes a by-product wastes that share of the atoms, however carefully it is done.

prompt: Ethene and steam make ethanol and nothing else: C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH. What is the atom economy of this reaction?
options: it cannot be known without doing the experiment
explain: Every atom in the reactants ends up in the one product, so desired mass ÷ total mass is 1, and 1 × 100 = 100%. A reaction with a single product always scores 100%.

md:
**The question.** In the blast furnace, $\ce{Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2}$. Calculate the atom economy for making iron, to one decimal place.
**Line 1, the desired product with its balancing number.** 2Fe: 2 × 56 = 112.
**Line 2, every product with its balancing number.** 3CO₂: 3 × 44 = 132, so the total is 112 + 132 = 244.

prompt: Finish the blast-furnace calculation: 112 ÷ 244 × 100, to one decimal place.
explain: 45.9%. Dropping the 2 in front of Fe gives 23.0%; dropping the 3 in front of CO₂ gives 71.8%. Balancing numbers are part of the masses.

md:
**Line 3, the percentage.** 112 ÷ 244 × 100 = **45.9%**.
**A free check.** The reactants add up to 160 + 3 × 28 = 244 as well. If your two totals disagree, a balancing number has gone missing.

prompt: In the thermite reaction, 2Al + Fe₂O₃ → 2Fe + Al₂O₃. Iron is the product wanted. What goes on top of the atom economy fraction?
explain: The equation makes two iron atoms, so the desired mass is 2 × 56 = 112. Aluminium is a reactant, and a reactant never goes on top.

md:
Copper(II) sulfate can be made from copper(II) oxide or from copper(II) carbonate. The carbonate route also makes carbon dioxide, so its atom economy is lower: 72.1% against 89.9%.
A high atom economy matters for two separate reasons, and a full answer gives both.
**Sustainable development:** fewer raw materials are used up to make the same product, and less waste is made.
**Economic:** less money goes on raw materials that end up as waste, and on getting rid of it.

prompt: Which of these is a reason for wanting a high atom economy that an examiner would credit?
explain: Atom economy is about atoms, not energy or speed. Less waste, fewer raw materials used up and lower costs are the reasons that earn marks.

title: Summer 2025 C2 Higher Q5
md: Asked why a laboratory preparation with a low atom economy was **not sustainable**, candidates struggled, and answers about **using less energy were not credited**. Argue from the atoms: raw materials used up, waste made, and what both cost.

title: GCSE Chemistry Revision "Atom Economy" (Triple)
why: A second explanation of the atom economy formula, worked on different reactions from the ones above. 'Triple' in the title is another board's label: for CCEA this is Higher Tier Double Award content.

prompt: A company switches to a route with a higher atom economy. Which of these is an economic reason for the switch?
options: less is spent on raw materials that end up as waste
fewer resources are used up for future generations
answer: less is spent on raw materials that end up as waste
explain: Money is the economic reason; resources for the future is the sustainable-development reason. A full answer to 'why does it matter' gives one of each.

text: 8. Atom economy is not percentage yield

alt: Two cards: atom economy compares the mass of the product wanted with the total mass of products and comes from the balanced equation; percentage yield compares the mass actually made with the most that could be made and comes from an experiment.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 740 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="cyvet"><title id="cyvet">Two cards. Atom economy compares the mass of the wanted product with the total mass of products, is worked out from the balanced equation and is known before the reaction is run. Percentage yield compares the mass actually made with the most that could be made, needs a real experiment and is lowered by losses, side reactions and reversible reactions.</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.5"><rect x="30" y="48" width="330" height="178" rx="8"/><rect x="380" y="48" width="330" height="178" rx="8"/></g><g font-family="inherit" font-size="13" fill="currentColor"><text x="30" y="28" font-size="14" font-weight="600">Two different questions about one reaction</text><text x="46" y="76" font-size="14" font-weight="600">Atom economy</text><text x="46" y="106" font-size="12">compares: the mass of the product wanted</text><text x="46" y="130" font-size="12">with the total mass of all the products</text><text x="46" y="154" font-size="12">worked out from: the balanced equation</text><text x="46" y="178" font-size="12">known: before the reaction is ever run</text><text x="46" y="202" font-size="12">lowered by: by-products the equation makes</text><text x="396" y="76" font-size="14" font-weight="600">Percentage yield</text><text x="396" y="106" font-size="12">compares: the mass of product actually made</text><text x="396" y="130" font-size="12">with the most that could have been made</text><text x="396" y="154" font-size="12">worked out from: a real experiment</text><text x="396" y="178" font-size="12">known: only after the reaction is run</text><text x="396" y="202" font-size="12">lowered by: losses, side reactions, reversibility</text></g></svg>
caption: Atom economy is decided on paper; percentage yield is decided in the laboratory.

md:
Both are percentages, and they answer different questions. **Atom economy** comes from the balanced equation: how much of the products' mass is the product you want. **Percentage yield** comes from an experiment: how much product you actually collected, compared with the most you could have made.
So a reaction can reach a 100% yield and still have a poor atom economy, because its by-products were built into the equation.

prompt: Heating calcium carbonate gives a 100% yield of calcium oxide. What is the atom economy for making calcium oxide?
explain: The yield says every possible gram of calcium oxide was collected; the atom economy still says 44 of every 100 mass units left as carbon dioxide. They measure different things.

md:
Convert a volume from cm³ to dm³ as the first line of working.
Calculate a concentration in mol/dm³ from a mass of solute and a volume.
Find the moles or the mass of solute in a volume of known concentration.
Calculate an atom economy from a balanced equation, balancing numbers included.
Give a sustainable-development reason and an economic reason for a high atom economy.

This is Higher Tier only, and the two halves often share one question. A mass or concentration calculation is **[2]** to **[3]**: the moles or the volume in dm³ first, the Mr, then the answer. An atom economy is **[3]**: the desired mass, the total mass of products, the percentage. Write every line, because a slip is carried forward. For *why is this not sustainable*, argue from wasted atoms and cost, never energy.
